records.source: Πρωΐας δὲ γενομένης συμβούλιον ἔλαβον πάντες οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι τοῦ λαοῦ κατὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ὥστε θανατῶσαι αὐτόν·
records.gloss: Morning then having come, counsel took all the chief priests and the elders of the people against the Jesus so as to put to death him;
pieces: Early in the morning all the chief priests and the elders of the people met and reached their decision against Jesus: {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} must be put to death.

L.1: Now when morning had come, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus, so as to put {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to death;

R.1: Early the next morning, all the leading priests and the elders of the people met together. They made a plan to have Jesus killed.

decisions.choice: took counsel: came to a decision together
decisions.reason: The phrase means to form a plan or reach a decision (12:14). After the hearing at night (26:57-68), the leaders now settle on their course.

decisions.choice: so as to put him to death: they needed the Roman governor to carry out the sentence
decisions.reason: Under Roman rule the Jewish council could not lawfully carry out an execution (John 18:31). So they took Jesus to Pilate (27:2).

decisions.choice: the next morning
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that this is the morning after the night hearing of chapter 26.

records.heading: Jesus handed over to Pilate

records.source: καὶ δήσαντες αὐτὸν ἀπήγαγον καὶ παρέδωκαν Πιλάτῳ τῷ ἡγεμόνι.
records.gloss: and having bound him they led away and handed over to Pilate the governor.
pieces: They tied {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} up, led {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} away, and handed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over to Pilate, the governor.

L.2: and having bound {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, they led [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] away and handed [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] over to Pilate the governor.

R.2: They tied {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} up and led {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} away. Then they handed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over to Pilate, the Roman governor.

decisions.choice: Pilate the governor: Pontius Pilate, Roman governor of Judea
decisions.reason: Pilate governed Judea for Rome from about AD 26 to 36. Only he could order an execution.

decisions.choice: handed over: the verb used all through for Jesus being given up
decisions.reason: Jesus had said he would be handed over to the chief priests and then to the Gentiles (17:22; 20:18-19). Both now happen.

decisions.choice: Pilate, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: Pontius Pilate, the reading of many later manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts give his full name, Pontius Pilate. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Roman governor
decisions.reason: Readable says whose governor Pilate was.

records.source: Τότε ἰδὼν Ἰούδας ὁ παραδιδοὺς αὐτὸν ὅτι κατεκρίθη μεταμεληθεὶς ἔστρεψεν τὰ τριάκοντα ἀργύρια τοῖς ἀρχιερεῦσιν καὶ πρεσβυτέροις λέγων· Ἥμαρτον παραδοὺς αἷμα ἀθῷον.
records.gloss: Then having seen Judas the [one] handing over him that he was condemned, having regretted he returned the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders \v 4 saying, I sinned having handed over blood innocent.
pieces: When Judas, who had betrayed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, saw that Jesus had been condemned, he was seized with regret and took the thirty silver coins back to the chief priests and the elders.
"I have sinned," he said. "I have handed an innocent man over to death."

L.3: Then Judas, the one who handed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over, seeing that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} had been condemned, regretted [it] and brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders,
L.4: saying, "I have sinned in handing over innocent blood."

R.3: Judas was the one who had handed Jesus over to the leaders. When he saw that Jesus had been sentenced to death, he felt terrible about what he had done. He took the thirty silver coins back to the leading priests and the elders.
R.4: He said, "I have sinned. I handed over a man who did nothing wrong, and now they will kill {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

decisions.choice: regretted: was filled with remorse
decisions.reason: The verb means to feel sorry afterward about what one has done. It is not the word for repentance in 3:2 and 4:17; Matthew uses it of a change of mind in 21:29, 32. Judas regrets his act, but the story does not say he turned to God.

decisions.choice: innocent blood: the life of an innocent person, given up to death
decisions.reason: Blood stands for a life taken by violence. The law puts a curse on anyone who takes a bribe to kill an innocent person (Deuteronomy 27:25).

decisions.choice: the thirty pieces of silver: the sum agreed in 26:15
decisions.reason: The coins were most likely silver shekels or coins of the same weight. Thirty was the price the law set for a slave (Exodus 21:32), about four months' wages for a laborer.

decisions.choice: innocent, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: righteous, the reading of some manuscripts
decisions.reason: Some manuscripts read "righteous blood". Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: who had betrayed him (B); handed Jesus over (R); handed an innocent man over to death (B)
alternatives: handed him over at every level
decisions.reason: The same verb means to hand over and, of a friend, to betray. Balanced calls Judas the betrayer, as 10:4 does, and says plainly what handing over innocent blood meant.

decisions.choice: thirty silver coins
decisions.reason: Readable uses plain words for the coins. The value is given in a meaning decision.

records.heading: Judas and the thirty pieces of silver

records.source: οἱ δὲ εἶπαν· Τί πρὸς ἡμᾶς;
records.gloss: They but said, What to us?
pieces: They answered, "Why should that concern us?

L.4: But they said, "What [is that] to us?

R.4: But they said, "We do not care about that.

decisions.choice: What is that to us: that is no concern of ours
decisions.reason: The question is a way of refusing. The leaders who paid Judas will take no share in his guilt.

decisions.choice: a statement
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question into the statement it means.

records.source: σὺ ὄψῃ.
records.gloss: You will see.
pieces: That is your affair."

decisions.choice: you will see to it: deal with it yourself
alternatives: a prediction that Judas will see something
decisions.reason: The future is used as a command: the matter is yours. Pilate says the same words to the crowd in 27:24.

decisions.choice: That is your affair (B); That is your problem (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the idiom.

records.source: καὶ ῥίψας τὰ ἀργύρια εἰς τὸν ναὸν ἀνεχώρησεν, καὶ ἀπελθὼν ἀπήγξατο.
records.gloss: And having thrown the pieces of silver into the temple he withdrew, and having gone away he hanged himself.
pieces: Judas flung the silver into the temple and left. Then he went away and hanged himself.

L.5: And throwing the pieces of silver into the temple, he left; and he went away and hanged himself.

R.5: Judas threw the money into the temple and left. Then he went off and hanged himself.

decisions.choice: into the temple: the word usually means the sanctuary itself
decisions.reason: Matthew's word usually means the sanctuary building, where only priests went. Judas may have thrown the coins into the court of the priests, or the word may be used loosely for the temple. Matthew does not say.

decisions.choice: he hanged himself: Matthew's account of Judas's death
decisions.reason: Acts 1:18-19 tells of Judas's death in other words and also speaks of a field called the Field of Blood. The text does not say how the two accounts fit together.

decisions.choice: the silver (B); the money (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable avoid repeating the full phrase from 27:3.

records.source: οἱ δὲ ἀρχιερεῖς λαβόντες τὰ ἀργύρια εἶπαν· Οὐκ ἔξεστιν βαλεῖν αὐτὰ εἰς τὸν κορβανᾶν, ἐπεὶ τιμὴ αἵματός ἐστιν·
records.gloss: The but chief priests having taken the pieces of silver said, Not it is lawful to put them into the treasury, since price of blood it is;
pieces: The chief priests gathered up the coins. "The law does not let us put this into the temple treasury," they said, "because it was paid to bring about a death."

L.6: But the chief priests took the pieces of silver and said, "It is not lawful to put them into the treasury, since it is [the] price of blood."

R.6: The leading priests picked up the money. They said, "Our law does not allow us to put this money in the temple treasury. It was paid to have a man killed."

decisions.choice: the treasury: the temple fund for offerings
decisions.reason: The word comes from the term for a gift given to God (Mark 7:11). The law forbade bringing money gained by sin into God's house as an offering (Deuteronomy 23:18).

decisions.choice: price of blood: money paid for a killing
decisions.reason: The phrase means the price paid to take a life. The priests speak of the money in the very terms Judas used in 27:4, though they had paid it themselves.

decisions.choice: paid to bring about a death (B); paid to have a man killed (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly what the idiom means.

records.source: συμβούλιον δὲ λαβόντες ἠγόρασαν ἐξ αὐτῶν τὸν Ἀγρὸν τοῦ Κεραμέως εἰς ταφὴν τοῖς ξένοις.
records.gloss: Counsel then having taken they bought with them the Field of the Potter for burial for the strangers.
pieces: They talked it over and decided to buy the Potter's Field with the money, as a place to bury people from other lands.

L.7: So after taking counsel, they bought with them the Potter's Field as a burial place for strangers.

R.7: They decided to use the money to buy a field known as the Potter's Field. It would be a place to bury people from other places who died in Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: the Potter's Field: a field known by that name
alternatives: any field owned by a potter
decisions.reason: The article shows a known place, perhaps where potters dug clay or worked. The name prepares for the quotation in 27:10.

decisions.choice: strangers: people from elsewhere, such as visitors and foreigners who died in the city
decisions.reason: The word means people who do not belong to the place. Pilgrims and foreigners who died in Jerusalem had no family grave there.

decisions.choice: people from other places who died in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable explains who the strangers were.

records.source: διὸ ἐκλήθη ὁ ἀγρὸς ἐκεῖνος Ἀγρὸς Αἵματος ἕως τῆς σήμερον.
records.gloss: Therefore was called the field that Field of Blood until the today.
pieces: This is why that field has had the name Field of Blood ever since, up to the present day.

L.8: Therefore that field has been called [the] Field of Blood to this day.

R.8: That is why people still call that place the Field of Blood.

decisions.choice: Field of Blood: named for the blood money that bought it
decisions.reason: The field was bought with the price of Jesus's death (27:6). Acts 1:19 gives the name in Aramaic, Hakeldama, and explains it from Judas's death.

decisions.choice: to this day: to the time when Matthew wrote
alternatives: to the day of the crucifixion
decisions.reason: The phrase tells the first readers that the name was still in use in their own time (compare 28:15).

records.source: τότε ἐπληρώθη τὸ ῥηθὲν διὰ Ἰερεμίου τοῦ προφήτου λέγοντος· Καὶ ἔλαβον τὰ τριάκοντα ἀργύρια, τὴν τιμὴν τοῦ τετιμημένου ὃν ἐτιμήσαντο ἀπὸ υἱῶν Ἰσραήλ, καὶ ἔδωκαν αὐτὰ εἰς τὸν ἀγρὸν τοῦ κεραμέως, καθὰ συνέταξέν μοι κύριος.
records.gloss: Then was fulfilled the [thing] spoken through Jeremiah the prophet saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the [one] having been priced, whom they priced from sons of Israel, \v 10 and they gave them for the field of the potter, as directed me Lord.
pieces: Then the word spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled: "They took the thirty silver coins, the price set on the one whose value some of the people of Israel had fixed,
and they gave them for the potter's field, as the Lord had instructed me."

L.9: Then what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled, saying, "And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of the one who had been priced, on whom [some] of [the] sons of Israel set a price,
L.10: and they gave them for the potter's field, as [the] Lord directed me."

R.9: This made what the prophet Jeremiah had said come true: "They took the thirty silver coins. That was the price some of the people of Israel put on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
R.10: They used the coins to buy the potter's field, as the Lord had told me."

decisions.choice: spoken through Jeremiah: the words are closest to Zechariah 11:12-13, joined with themes from Jeremiah
decisions.reason: The thirty pieces of silver, the price set, and the money thrown to the potter in the temple come from Zechariah 11:12-13. Jeremiah goes to a potter's house (18:1-12), breaks a potter's jar at a valley to be renamed for slaughter and burial (19:1-13), and buys a field with silver (32:6-15). Matthew may name Jeremiah as the better-known prophet whose themes shape the combined words. Why he names only Jeremiah is not certain.

decisions.choice: Jeremiah, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: Zechariah, or no name, in a few manuscripts
decisions.reason: A few manuscripts read "Zechariah" or leave the name out, which looks like an attempt to ease the difficulty. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: they took, they gave: the leaders are the ones who acted
alternatives: I took, I gave, as in Zechariah 11:13
decisions.reason: The first verb can mean "I took" or "they took". The SBLGNT reads "they gave" in 27:10, so the sentence reads best as the leaders' actions, which Matthew has just told. Some manuscripts read "I gave".

decisions.choice: as the Lord directed me: the Lord is God, whose name stands in the Hebrew
decisions.reason: The closing words echo the way Scripture speaks of doing what God commanded. In Zechariah 11:13 the Hebrew has God's name, which the Greek Old Testament gives as "Lord".

decisions.choice: the people of Israel
decisions.reason: The phrase means Israelites. Literal keeps "sons"; those who set the price were men, so no setting applies.

decisions.choice: the price as a sentence of its own, with him for the one priced
alternatives: the price of the one who had been priced
decisions.reason: Readable breaks up the play on words and makes plain that the one priced is Jesus, so the pronoun takes the deity_pronoun setting.

records.source: Ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἐστάθη ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ ἡγεμόνος· καὶ ἐπηρώτησεν αὐτὸν ὁ ἡγεμὼν λέγων· Σὺ εἶ ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων;
records.gloss: The but Jesus stood before the governor; and asked him the governor saying, You are the King of the Jews?
pieces: Jesus now stood in front of the governor, who questioned {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}: "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the King of the Jews?"

L.11: Now Jesus stood before the governor, and the governor questioned {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, saying, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the King of the Jews?"

R.11: Jesus stood in front of Pilate, the governor. Pilate asked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Are {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} the King of the Jews?"

decisions.choice: the King of the Jews: a political charge
decisions.reason: Rome alone appointed kings. A man called king without Rome's approval was a rebel. The magi used the same title at Jesus's birth (2:2), and it will be the charge over the cross (27:37).

decisions.choice: you: stressed
decisions.reason: The pronoun is written out: you, this prisoner, are the king?

decisions.choice: King, capitalized
decisions.reason: In this chapter the words are a title, the charge written over the cross (27:37), so King is capitalized at every level. Readable names Pilate.

records.heading: Jesus before the governor

records.source: ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἔφη· Σὺ λέγεις.
records.gloss: The but Jesus said, You say.
pieces: Jesus replied, "It is you who say it."

R.11: Jesus answered, "You are the one saying that."

decisions.choice: You say so: a guarded yes, which leaves the words in Pilate's mouth
decisions.reason: Jesus does not deny the title, but he does not take up Pilate's meaning either. He answered Judas and the high priest in a similar way, with the past tense of the same verb (26:25, 64). The kind of king Pilate fears is not what Jesus is.

decisions.choice: You: stressed, it is Pilate who says it
decisions.reason: The pronoun is written out, putting weight on Pilate as the speaker. Jesus speaks to Pilate, so the pronoun takes no setting.

decisions.choice: It is you who say it (B); You are the one saying that (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the guarded form of the answer and do not turn it into a plain yes.

records.source: καὶ ἐν τῷ κατηγορεῖσθαι αὐτὸν ὑπὸ τῶν ἀρχιερέων καὶ πρεσβυτέρων οὐδὲν ἀπεκρίνατο.
records.gloss: And in the being accused him by the chief priests and elders nothing he answered.
pieces: But when the chief priests and the elders brought their charges against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} made no reply.

L.12: And while {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was being accused by the chief priests and elders, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} answered nothing.

R.12: The leading priests and the elders kept accusing {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said nothing in reply.

decisions.choice: he answered nothing: perhaps Isaiah 53:7
decisions.reason: The servant in Isaiah 53:7 was silent like a sheep before its shearers. Jesus was silent before the council too (26:63). Matthew does not cite the verse here.

decisions.choice: while he was being accused: the charges went on
decisions.reason: The construction describes the accusing as it went on, perhaps charge after charge (27:13).

records.source: τότε λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Οὐκ ἀκούεις πόσα σου καταμαρτυροῦσιν;
records.gloss: Then says to him the Pilate, Not do you hear how many things against you they testify?
pieces: Then Pilate said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} not hear all the charges they are bringing against {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}?"

L.13: Then Pilate says to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "Do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} not hear how many things they testify against {{deity_pronoun:you|You}}?"

R.13: So Pilate said to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, "They are accusing {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} of so many things. Do {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} not hear them?"

decisions.choice: testify against: bring evidence against, accuse
decisions.reason: The verb is used of witnesses giving evidence against someone in court, as at the night hearing (26:62).

decisions.choice: present tense of narration (L); past (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek present tense of narration.

records.source: καὶ οὐκ ἀπεκρίθη αὐτῷ πρὸς οὐδὲ ἓν ῥῆμα, ὥστε θαυμάζειν τὸν ἡγεμόνα λίαν.
records.gloss: And not he answered him to not even one word, so as to marvel the governor greatly.
pieces: Still Jesus did not answer him on even one point, and the governor was deeply amazed at this.

L.14: And {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did not answer him, not even to one word, so that the governor was greatly amazed.

R.14: But Jesus did not say one word to answer him. The governor was very surprised.

decisions.choice: word: point or charge
decisions.reason: The noun can mean a word or a matter. Jesus did not answer a single one of the charges.

decisions.choice: the governor was amazed: Jesus's silence surprised him
decisions.reason: Prisoners facing death usually defended themselves. Jesus's silence left Pilate wondering.

decisions.choice: Jesus
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus, since the sentence before ended with Pilate speaking.

records.source: Κατὰ δὲ ἑορτὴν εἰώθει ὁ ἡγεμὼν ἀπολύειν ἕνα τῷ ὄχλῳ δέσμιον ὃν ἤθελον.
records.gloss: At now feast was accustomed the governor to release one to the crowd prisoner whom they wanted.
pieces: At each festival the governor used to set free one prisoner for the crowd, whichever one they wanted.

L.15: Now at [the] feast the governor was accustomed to release to the crowd one prisoner, whom they wanted.

R.15: Each year at the Passover festival, the governor would let one prisoner go free. The crowd could choose which prisoner it would be.

decisions.choice: the feast: the Passover
decisions.reason: The story has been set at the Passover since 26:2. The custom belonged to this feast.

decisions.choice: the release of a prisoner: a custom known only from the Gospels
decisions.reason: No other ancient writer mentions this custom, but all four Gospels do (Mark 15:6; John 18:39). It was a favor to the people at their festival.

decisions.choice: Each year at the Passover festival
decisions.reason: Readable names the feast and makes the yearly custom clear.

records.source: εἶχον δὲ τότε δέσμιον ἐπίσημον λεγόμενον Ἰησοῦν Βαραββᾶν.
records.gloss: They were having then at that time a prisoner notorious called Jesus Barabbas.
pieces: At that time they were holding a prisoner everyone knew of, called Jesus Barabbas.

L.16: And at that time they had a notorious prisoner called Jesus Barabbas.

R.16: At that time there was a well-known prisoner named Jesus Barabbas.

decisions.choice: Jesus Barabbas, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: Barabbas, the reading of most manuscripts
decisions.reason: Most manuscripts have only "Barabbas" here and in 27:17. A few manuscripts and some early translations read "Jesus Barabbas", and the SBLGNT follows them. Jesus was a common name, and copyists were more likely to drop it from a criminal than to add it. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Barabbas: an Aramaic name meaning son of the father
decisions.reason: Bar means son and abba means father. It was a family name. Mark 15:7 says he was held with rebels who had committed murder.

decisions.choice: notorious: well known, here for his crimes
decisions.reason: The word means marked out or famous. Mark 15:7 and Luke 23:19 tell of rebellion and murder.

decisions.choice: a prisoner everyone knew of (B); a well-known prisoner (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use everyday words for a prisoner whose name was widely known.

records.source: συνηγμένων οὖν αὐτῶν εἶπεν αὐτοῖς ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Τίνα θέλετε ἀπολύσω ὑμῖν, Ἰησοῦν τὸν Βαραββᾶν ἢ Ἰησοῦν τὸν λεγόμενον χριστόν;
records.gloss: Having been gathered therefore of them said to them the Pilate, Whom do you want I release to you, Jesus the Barabbas or Jesus the [one] called Christ?
pieces: When the crowd had gathered, Pilate asked them, "Which one do you want me to set free for you: Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus who is called {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}?"

L.17: So when they had gathered, Pilate said to them, "Whom do you want me to release to you, Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus, the [one] called {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}?"

R.17: So when the people had come together, Pilate asked them, "Which man do you want me to set free? Should it be Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus, the one people call {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}?"

decisions.choice: Jesus Barabbas, as in 27:16
alternatives: Barabbas, the reading of most manuscripts
decisions.reason: Most manuscripts read only "Barabbas" here too; see the note at 27:16. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: who is called Christ: Pilate repeats what others say of Jesus
decisions.reason: As in 1:16 the phrase gives the name people know him by. Pilate does not say he believes it.

decisions.choice: two men named Jesus set side by side
decisions.reason: If the SBLGNT reading is right, the crowd must choose between two men named Jesus: one called son of the father, the other called the Messiah.

decisions.choice: the one people call
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that the title is what people were saying about Jesus.

records.source: ᾔδει γὰρ ὅτι διὰ φθόνον παρέδωκαν αὐτόν.
records.gloss: He knew for that because of envy they had handed over him.
pieces: He was aware that envy had moved them to hand Jesus over.

L.18: For he knew that it was out of envy that they had handed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over.

R.18: Pilate knew that the leaders had brought Jesus to him because they were jealous of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: envy: resentment of the following Jesus had among the people
decisions.reason: The leaders had feared the crowds who held Jesus to be a prophet (21:46) and resented the praise he received (21:15-16).

decisions.choice: they: the chief priests and elders
decisions.reason: Those who handed Jesus over were the leaders (27:1-2).

decisions.choice: the leaders
decisions.reason: Readable says who handed Jesus over.

records.source: Καθημένου δὲ αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τοῦ βήματος ἀπέστειλεν πρὸς αὐτὸν ἡ γυνὴ αὐτοῦ λέγουσα· Μηδὲν σοὶ καὶ τῷ δικαίῳ ἐκείνῳ, πολλὰ γὰρ ἔπαθον σήμερον κατ’ ὄναρ δι’ αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Sitting then of him on the judgment seat sent to him the wife of him saying, Nothing to you and to the righteous that; many things for I suffered today in a dream because of him.
pieces: As Pilate sat on the judgment seat, a message came to him from his wife: "Leave that righteous man alone. Today in a dream I went through great distress over {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

L.19: Now while he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent [word] to him, saying, "[Have] nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

R.19: Pilate was sitting in his place as judge. While he was there, his wife sent him a message. It said, "Do not have anything to do with that man. He is innocent. Today I had a dream about {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and it troubled me very much."

decisions.choice: the judgment seat: the raised platform where a Roman official sat to give judgment
decisions.reason: Pilate is acting as judge in a formal hearing.

decisions.choice: righteous: innocent, in the right
decisions.reason: In a court the word means one who is in the right and not guilty. Pilate's wife declares Jesus innocent, as Pilate himself soon claims to be (27:24).

decisions.choice: a dream: a warning sent in a dream
decisions.reason: Matthew tells of God guiding people by dreams (1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22). Here the dream warns of Jesus's innocence. Matthew does not say what she saw.

decisions.choice: He is innocent
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense the word has in a court. The pronoun begins a sentence, so it is written plain.

decisions.choice: sent [word]
decisions.reason: Literal supplies what she sent.

records.source: Οἱ δὲ ἀρχιερεῖς καὶ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι ἔπεισαν τοὺς ὄχλους ἵνα αἰτήσωνται τὸν Βαραββᾶν τὸν δὲ Ἰησοῦν ἀπολέσωσιν.
records.gloss: The but chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds that they should ask for the Barabbas, the but Jesus they should destroy.
pieces: But the chief priests and the elders talked the crowds into asking for Barabbas and having Jesus put to death.

L.20: But the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and to destroy Jesus.

R.20: But the leading priests and the elders talked the people into asking Pilate to free Barabbas and to have Jesus killed.

decisions.choice: destroy: have him put to death
decisions.reason: The verb means to destroy or kill. The crowds could only ask; Pilate would give the order.

decisions.choice: the crowds: the people gathered at the governor's residence
decisions.reason: Matthew speaks of the crowds present that morning, whom the leaders persuaded. This shapes how 27:25 should be read.

decisions.choice: having Jesus put to death (B); to have Jesus killed (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what destroying him meant.

records.source: ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ ὁ ἡγεμὼν εἶπεν αὐτοῖς· Τίνα θέλετε ἀπὸ τῶν δύο ἀπολύσω ὑμῖν;
records.gloss: Answering then the governor said to them, Whom do you want from the two I release to you?
pieces: The governor asked them again, "Which of these two do you want me to set free for you?"

L.21: And the governor answered and said to them, "Which of the two do you want me to release to you?"

R.21: The governor asked the people, "Which of these two men do you want me to set free?"

decisions.choice: answered: responded to the situation, not to a question
decisions.reason: The word often introduces speech without a question before it (11:25). Pilate responds to the crowd's growing pressure.

decisions.choice: again
decisions.reason: Balanced shows that Pilate is repeating the question of 27:17.

records.source: οἱ δὲ εἶπαν· Τὸν Βαραββᾶν.
records.gloss: They but said, The Barabbas.
pieces: "Barabbas!" they said.

decisions.choice: Barabbas: the name alone
decisions.reason: From here on the SBLGNT, like all manuscripts, uses only the name Barabbas. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

records.source: λέγει αὐτοῖς ὁ Πιλᾶτος· Τί οὖν ποιήσω Ἰησοῦν τὸν λεγόμενον χριστόν;
records.gloss: Says to them the Pilate, What then shall I do [with] Jesus the [one] called Christ?
pieces: Pilate asked them, "Then what am I to do with Jesus who is called {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}?"

L.22: Pilate says to them, "Then what shall I do with Jesus, the [one] called {{christos:Christ|Messiah}}?"

R.22: Pilate asked, "Then what should I do with Jesus, the one people call {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}?"

decisions.choice: what shall I do: a real question for the crowd
decisions.reason: Pilate puts the decision in the crowd's hands, as he will again in 27:24.

decisions.choice: present tense of narration (L); past (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek present tense of narration.

records.source: λέγουσιν πάντες· Σταυρωθήτω.
records.gloss: They say all, Let him be crucified.
pieces: They all shouted, "Let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} be crucified!"

R.22: All of them shouted, "Have {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} killed on a cross!"

decisions.choice: crucified: put to death on a cross
decisions.reason: Crucifixion was the Roman death for slaves and rebels. It was slow and shameful, carried out in public as a warning. Jesus had foretold it (20:19).

decisions.choice: present tense of narration (L); past (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek present tense of narration.

decisions.choice: Have him killed on a cross
decisions.reason: Readable says what crucifixion was.

records.source: ὁ δὲ ἔφη· Τί γὰρ κακὸν ἐποίησεν;
records.gloss: The but said, What for evil did he do?
pieces: "But what wrong has {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} done?" Pilate asked.

L.23: But he said, "Why, what evil has {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} done?"

R.23: Pilate asked, "Why? What bad thing has this man done?"

decisions.choice: for: a word of protest, why, what then
decisions.reason: In a question the word adds force: why, what has he done?

decisions.choice: Pilate
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the speaker.

records.source: οἱ δὲ περισσῶς ἔκραζον λέγοντες· Σταυρωθήτω.
records.gloss: They but all the more were crying out saying, Let him be crucified.
pieces: But they only shouted louder and louder, "Let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} be crucified!"

L.23: But they kept crying out all the more, saying, "Let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} be crucified!"

R.23: But the people shouted even louder, "Have {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} killed on a cross!"

decisions.choice: kept crying out all the more: the shouting grew and went on
decisions.reason: The tense shows a shout repeated again and again, growing louder.

records.source: ἰδὼν δὲ ὁ Πιλᾶτος ὅτι οὐδὲν ὠφελεῖ ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον θόρυβος γίνεται λαβὼν ὕδωρ ἀπενίψατο τὰς χεῖρας ἀπέναντι τοῦ ὄχλου λέγων· Ἀθῷός εἰμι ἀπὸ τοῦ αἵματος τούτου· ὑμεῖς ὄψεσθε.
records.gloss: Having seen then the Pilate that nothing it avails but rather a riot is arising, having taken water he washed the hands before the crowd saying, Innocent I am of the blood this; you will see.
pieces: Pilate saw that he was getting nowhere and that an uproar was starting instead. So he took water and washed his hands in front of the crowd. "I am not guilty of this man's death," he said. "That is your affair."

L.24: And when Pilate saw that he was gaining nothing, but rather a riot was starting, he took water and washed [his] hands before the crowd, saying, "I am innocent of this blood; you will see [to it]."

R.24: Pilate saw that he could not change their minds. Instead, the crowd was starting to riot. So he took some water and washed his hands in front of them. He said, "I am not to blame for this man's death. You are responsible for it."

decisions.choice: washing the hands: a sign of declaring oneself innocent of a death
decisions.reason: The law gives this act to the elders of a town after an unsolved killing (Deuteronomy 21:6-9), and the psalms speak of washing the hands in innocence (Psalm 26:6; 73:13). Pilate uses a sign the crowd would understand.

decisions.choice: this blood: the blood of this man
decisions.reason: The words can be read "this blood" or "the blood of this man". Either way they mean Jesus's death.

decisions.choice: of this blood, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: of the blood of this righteous man, the reading of many manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts read "of the blood of this righteous man", echoing 27:19. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: you will see to it: the responsibility is yours
decisions.reason: Pilate uses the words the priests used to Judas in 27:4, and passes the matter to the crowd. Washing his hands does not undo his own order (27:26).

decisions.choice: not guilty of this man's death (B); not to blame for this man's death (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly what the idiom of blood means.

records.source: καὶ ἀποκριθεὶς πᾶς ὁ λαὸς εἶπεν· Τὸ αἷμα αὐτοῦ ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ τέκνα ἡμῶν.
records.gloss: And answering all the people said, The blood of him on us and on the children of us.
pieces: All the people there answered, "Let the guilt for {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death fall on us and on our children!"

L.25: And all the people answered and said, "His blood [be] on us and on our children!"

R.25: All the people there shouted back, "We and our children will take the blame for {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} death!"

decisions.choice: his blood be on us: we accept the guilt for his death
alternatives: a wish to be cleansed by his blood
decisions.reason: The phrase takes on responsibility for a death (2 Samuel 1:16; Jeremiah 26:15; Acts 5:28). The crowd answers Pilate's claim to be innocent of this blood (27:24).

decisions.choice: the cry of this crowd at that moment
alternatives: a curse on the Jewish people for all time
decisions.reason: The words are the shout of the crowd gathered before Pilate that morning, whom their leaders had persuaded (27:20). Matthew reports what they said. The verse has been used to blame the Jewish people as a whole for Jesus's death and to justify hatred of Jews; the text does not support that use. Jesus, his disciples and the women at the cross were Jews, and in Matthew Jesus's blood is poured out for the forgiveness of sins for many (26:28).

decisions.choice: all the people: those present who answered Pilate
decisions.reason: Matthew here uses the word "people", often used of Israel, in place of "crowd". The context limits it to those who stood before Pilate and answered him. Some read the change of word as making the crowd stand for the nation; the sentence itself speaks of those present.

decisions.choice: Let the guilt for his death fall on us (B); take the blame for his death (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the idiom means. Literal keeps the words of the cry.

decisions.choice: there
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that the people are those present.

records.source: τότε ἀπέλυσεν αὐτοῖς τὸν Βαραββᾶν, τὸν δὲ Ἰησοῦν φραγελλώσας παρέδωκεν ἵνα σταυρωθῇ.
records.gloss: Then he released to them the Barabbas, the but Jesus having flogged he handed over that he might be crucified.
pieces: So Pilate let Barabbas go free, as they wanted. As for Jesus, Pilate ordered {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to be scourged, and then handed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over for crucifixion.

L.26: Then he released Barabbas to them, but after having Jesus flogged, he handed [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] over to be crucified.

R.26: Then Pilate set Barabbas free for the people. He had his soldiers beat Jesus with whips. Then he handed Jesus over to be killed on a cross.

decisions.choice: flogged: beaten with a Roman whip
decisions.reason: The Roman whip had leather straps weighted with bits of bone or metal. Flogging came before crucifixion and left the victim badly weakened. Jesus had foretold it (20:19).

decisions.choice: handed over: the verb used all through for Jesus being given up
decisions.reason: Judas handed him to the leaders, the leaders handed him to Pilate (27:2), and now Pilate hands him over to death, as Jesus had said (20:18-19; 26:2).

decisions.choice: Pilate ordered (B); had his soldiers (R); as they wanted (B)
decisions.reason: Pilate gave the order; his soldiers did the flogging. Balanced and Readable say so.

records.source: Τότε οἱ στρατιῶται τοῦ ἡγεμόνος παραλαβόντες τὸν Ἰησοῦν εἰς τὸ πραιτώριον συνήγαγον ἐπ’ αὐτὸν ὅλην τὴν σπεῖραν.
records.gloss: Then the soldiers of the governor having taken the Jesus into the praetorium gathered against him whole the cohort.
pieces: The governor's soldiers then brought Jesus inside the governor's headquarters, and the entire cohort assembled around {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.27: Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the praetorium and gathered the whole cohort around {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.27: Then Pilate's soldiers took Jesus into the governor's palace. All the soldiers in the unit gathered around {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: the praetorium: the governor's residence in Jerusalem
decisions.reason: The Latin word meant a commander's headquarters. In Jerusalem it was most likely Herod's former palace, or perhaps the Antonia fortress beside the temple.

decisions.choice: the cohort: the soldiers on hand
alternatives: a full unit of six hundred
decisions.reason: The word names a Roman unit of up to six hundred men. Matthew may mean all the soldiers present.

decisions.choice: around him: against him, gathered to mock him
decisions.reason: The phrase can mean around or against. The soldiers gather to make sport of him.

decisions.choice: headquarters, cohort (B); palace, unit (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use English words for the Roman terms.

records.heading: The soldiers mock the King of the Jews

records.source: καὶ ἐκδύσαντες αὐτὸν χλαμύδα κοκκίνην περιέθηκαν αὐτῷ, καὶ πλέξαντες στέφανον ἐξ ἀκανθῶν ἐπέθηκαν ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτοῦ καὶ κάλαμον ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ αὐτοῦ, καὶ γονυπετήσαντες ἔμπροσθεν αὐτοῦ ἐνέπαιξαν αὐτῷ λέγοντες· Χαῖρε, βασιλεῦ τῶν Ἰουδαίων, καὶ ἐμπτύσαντες εἰς αὐτὸν ἔλαβον τὸν κάλαμον καὶ ἔτυπτον εἰς τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: And having stripped him a robe scarlet they put around him, \v 29 and having woven a crown out of thorns they put on the head of him and a reed in the right of him, and having knelt before him they mocked him saying, Hail, King of the Jews, \v 30 and having spit on him they took the reed and were striking on the head of him.
pieces: They took off {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clothes and put a scarlet military cloak on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

They twisted thorny branches into a crown and set it on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head, and put a stick in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right hand. Then they went down on their knees in front of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and made fun of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}: "Hail, King of the Jews!"
They spat on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and took the stick and beat {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} over the head with it again and again.

L.28: And they stripped {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and put a scarlet robe around {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}},
L.29: and having woven a crown out of thorns, they put [it] on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head, and a reed in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right [hand]; and kneeling before {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, they mocked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!"
L.30: And they spat on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, took the reed, and kept striking [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head.

R.28: They took off {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clothes and put a red robe on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.
R.29: They made a crown out of thorny branches and pushed it onto {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head. They put a stick in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right hand, like a king's scepter. Then they knelt in front of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and laughed at {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. They said, "Long live the King of the Jews!"
R.30: They spat on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. Then they took the stick and kept hitting {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} on the head with it.

decisions.choice: a scarlet robe: a soldier's red cloak, put on him to mock him as a king
decisions.reason: The word names a short military cloak. Its red color imitated the purple worn by kings; Mark 15:17 calls it purple.

decisions.choice: a crown of thorns and a reed: a mock crown and scepter
decisions.reason: The crown and the reed in his right hand made fun of his claim to be king. Whether the thorns were also meant to hurt, Matthew does not say.

decisions.choice: Hail: the greeting given to an emperor
decisions.reason: Soldiers greeted the emperor with "Hail, Caesar". They use the royal greeting in scorn, as Jesus had said they would mock him (20:19).

decisions.choice: spitting and striking: perhaps Isaiah 50:6
decisions.reason: The servant in Isaiah 50:6 gives his back to those who strike him and does not hide his face from spitting. Matthew does not cite it.

decisions.choice: stick
decisions.reason: The word means a reed or a cane. Balanced and Readable say stick, as for the same word in 27:48.

decisions.choice: Long live; like a king's scepter
decisions.reason: Readable uses a greeting still given to kings and says what the stick stood for.

records.source: καὶ ὅτε ἐνέπαιξαν αὐτῷ, ἐξέδυσαν αὐτὸν τὴν χλαμύδα καὶ ἐνέδυσαν αὐτὸν τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀπήγαγον αὐτὸν εἰς τὸ σταυρῶσαι.
records.gloss: And when they had mocked him, they took off him the robe and put on him the garments of him and led away him to crucify.
pieces: After they had finished mocking {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, they stripped off the cloak and dressed {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} again in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own clothes. Then they led {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} out to be crucified.

L.31: And when they had mocked {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, they took the robe off {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} garments on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and led {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} away to crucify [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}].

R.31: When they finished making fun of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, they took off the red robe. They put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own clothes back on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. Then they took {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} away to kill {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} on a cross.

decisions.choice: his garments: his outer clothes
decisions.reason: The word means outer clothing. These are the clothes the soldiers will divide in 27:35.

decisions.choice: led him away to crucify him: the goal of the march
decisions.reason: The phrase states the purpose. The execution was carried out by the same soldiers.

decisions.choice: own
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that these are his own clothes, not the mock robe.

records.source: Ἐξερχόμενοι δὲ εὗρον ἄνθρωπον Κυρηναῖον ὀνόματι Σίμωνα· τοῦτον ἠγγάρευσαν ἵνα ἄρῃ τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: Going out then they found a man of Cyrene by name Simon; this one they compelled that he might carry the cross of him.
pieces: On their way out they came across a man from Cyrene named Simon, and they forced him to carry Jesus's cross.

L.32: And as they were going out, they found a man of Cyrene named Simon; this [man] they compelled to carry {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} cross.

R.32: As they were going out of the city, they met a man named Simon. He was from the city of Cyrene in North Africa. The soldiers forced him to carry Jesus's cross.

decisions.choice: compelled: forced into service, as Roman soldiers could
decisions.reason: Roman soldiers had the right to make a civilian carry a load for them. It is the verb Jesus used in 5:41.

decisions.choice: of Cyrene: from Cyrene, a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community
decisions.reason: Jews from Cyrene had their own synagogue in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9). Simon may have come for the Passover.

decisions.choice: the cross: probably the crossbeam carried by the condemned man
decisions.reason: The condemned man usually carried the crossbeam to the place of execution. John 19:17 says Jesus carried it at first; weakened by the flogging, he could not go on.

decisions.choice: going out: out of the city
decisions.reason: Executions took place outside the city walls (John 19:17, 20; Hebrews 13:12).

decisions.choice: compelled (L); forced (B)
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced use the same words as in 5:41, compels and forces.

decisions.choice: of the city; in North Africa; the soldiers
decisions.reason: Readable says where they went out from, where Cyrene was, and who forced Simon.

records.heading: Jesus is crucified

records.source: Καὶ ἐλθόντες εἰς τόπον λεγόμενον Γολγοθᾶ, ὅ ἐστιν Κρανίου Τόπος λεγόμενος, ἔδωκαν αὐτῷ πιεῖν οἶνον μετὰ χολῆς μεμιγμένον· καὶ γευσάμενος οὐκ ἠθέλησεν πιεῖν.
records.gloss: And having come to a place called Golgotha, which is of a skull place called, \v 34 they gave him to drink wine with gall mixed; and having tasted not he wanted to drink.
pieces: They arrived at a place named Golgotha, a name meaning Place of a Skull.
They gave {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} wine to drink that had gall mixed into it. He tasted it but would not drink it.

L.33: And coming to a place called Golgotha, which is called Place of a Skull,
L.34: they gave {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} wine mixed with gall to drink; and having tasted [it], {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was not willing to drink [it].

R.33: They came to a place called Golgotha. That name means "the Place of the Skull."
R.34: There the soldiers gave Jesus some wine mixed with something bitter. When {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} tasted it, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} would not drink it.

decisions.choice: Golgotha: an Aramaic word for skull
decisions.reason: Matthew gives the Aramaic name and then its meaning. Why the place had this name is not known: perhaps from the shape of the rock, or from its use for executions.

decisions.choice: wine mixed with gall: Psalm 69:21 (69:22 in the Hebrew numbering)
decisions.reason: The psalm says: they gave me gall for food, and for my thirst sour wine to drink. Gall is a bitter substance. Mark 15:23 calls the drink wine mixed with myrrh.

decisions.choice: he would not drink: he tasted it and refused
decisions.reason: The drink may have been meant to dull the pain (Proverbs 31:6), or to add to the mockery with its bitterness. Jesus had said he would not drink wine again until the kingdom (26:29). Matthew does not say why he refused.

decisions.choice: wine, the reading of the SBLGNT
alternatives: sour wine, the reading of many later manuscripts
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts read "sour wine", closer to the words of Psalm 69. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the soldiers; something bitter
decisions.reason: Readable names who gave the drink and explains gall in plain words.

records.source: σταυρώσαντες δὲ αὐτὸν διεμερίσαντο τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτοῦ βάλλοντες κλῆρον, καὶ καθήμενοι ἐτήρουν αὐτὸν ἐκεῖ.
records.gloss: Having crucified then him they divided the garments of him casting a lot, \v 36 and sitting they were keeping watch over him there.
pieces: When they had crucified {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, they shared out {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clothes among themselves by drawing lots.
Then they sat down there and kept guard over {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.35: And when they had crucified {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, they divided {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} garments among themselves by casting lots,
L.36: and sitting down, they kept watch over {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} there.

R.35: The soldiers nailed Jesus to the cross. Then they threw dice to decide which of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} clothes each of them would get.
R.36: After that, they sat down there to guard {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: dividing his garments, casting lots: Psalm 22:18 (22:19 in the Hebrew numbering)
decisions.reason: The psalm says: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots. Matthew tells the event in the psalm's words without quoting it.

decisions.choice: no quotation here in the SBLGNT
alternatives: many later manuscripts add: so that what was spoken by the prophet might be fulfilled, They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots
decisions.reason: Many later manuscripts add the fulfillment of Psalm 22:18 here, in words like John 19:24. The earliest manuscripts do not have it, and the SBLGNT leaves it out. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: dividing the garments: the executioners kept the clothes of the condemned
decisions.reason: The condemned were crucified naked or nearly so, and their clothes went to the soldiers.

decisions.choice: kept watch: guarded him so that no one took him down before he died
decisions.reason: Soldiers stayed by a cross until the condemned man was dead.

decisions.choice: drawing lots (B); threw dice (R)
decisions.reason: Lots were small marked objects thrown to decide by chance. Readable uses a familiar game of chance.

decisions.choice: nailed Jesus to the cross
decisions.reason: Readable says how crucifixion was done; John 20:25 tells of the nail marks in his hands.

records.source: καὶ ἐπέθηκαν ἐπάνω τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτοῦ τὴν αἰτίαν αὐτοῦ γεγραμμένην· Οὗτός ἐστιν Ἰησοῦς ὁ βασιλεὺς τῶν Ἰουδαίων.
records.gloss: And they put above the head of him the charge of him having been written: This is Jesus the King of the Jews.
pieces: Over {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head they placed the charge against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in writing: "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews."

L.37: And above {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head they put up the charge against {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, written: "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews."

R.37: Above {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} head they put a sign that told why {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was being killed. It said, "This is Jesus, the King of the Jews."

decisions.choice: the charge: a written notice of the crime
decisions.reason: A notice giving the crime was often carried before the condemned or fixed to the cross. The charge was claiming to be king, a crime against Rome (27:11).

decisions.choice: the King of the Jews: a mocking charge that Matthew presents as true
decisions.reason: Jesus was greeted with this title at his birth (2:2). The Romans wrote it in scorn; Matthew's readers know Jesus is the king it names.

decisions.choice: a sign that told why he was being killed
decisions.reason: Readable explains what the charge was.

records.source: Τότε σταυροῦνται σὺν αὐτῷ δύο λῃσταί, εἷς ἐκ δεξιῶν καὶ εἷς ἐξ εὐωνύμων.
records.gloss: Then are crucified with him two bandits, one on right and one on left.
pieces: Two bandits were crucified along with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, one at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right and the other at {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} left.

L.38: Then two bandits are crucified with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, one on [the] right and one on [the] left.

R.38: Two robbers were also killed on crosses next to Jesus. One was on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} right side, and the other was on {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} left.

decisions.choice: bandits: robbers, or violent rebels
decisions.reason: The word is used of armed robbers and of rebels who took up arms against Rome. It is stronger than thief.

decisions.choice: one on the right and one on the left: perhaps an echo of 20:21
decisions.reason: The mother of Zebedee's sons asked that her sons sit at Jesus's right and left in his kingdom (20:21-23). The places beside the king are now crosses.

decisions.choice: crucified with bandits: perhaps Isaiah 53:12
decisions.reason: The servant in Isaiah 53:12 is counted among wrongdoers. Matthew does not cite the verse.

decisions.choice: present tense of narration (L); past (B, R)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the Greek present tense of narration.

decisions.choice: robbers
decisions.reason: Readable uses a common word.

records.source: οἱ δὲ παραπορευόμενοι ἐβλασφήμουν αὐτὸν κινοῦντες τὰς κεφαλὰς αὐτῶν καὶ λέγοντες· Ὁ καταλύων τὸν ναὸν καὶ ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις οἰκοδομῶν, σῶσον σεαυτόν· εἰ υἱὸς εἶ τοῦ θεοῦ, κατάβηθι ἀπὸ τοῦ σταυροῦ.
records.gloss: Those then passing by were blaspheming him shaking the heads of them \v 40 and saying, The [one] destroying the temple and in three days building, save yourself; if son you are of the God, come down from the cross.
pieces: People going past heaped insults on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and shook their heads.

"So {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} were going to tear down the temple and build it again in three days!" they said. "Save {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}! If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the Son of God, come down from the cross!"

L.39: And those passing by were reviling {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, shaking their heads
L.40: and saying, "You who destroy the temple and build [it] in three days, save {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}! If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are [the] Son of God, come down from the cross."

R.39: People who walked by insulted {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. They shook their heads at {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
R.40: and said, "You said {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} would destroy the temple and build it again in three days. So save {{deity_pronoun:yourself|Yourself}}! If {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} are the Son of God, come down from the cross!"

decisions.choice: reviling: speaking insults
decisions.reason: The verb means to speak abusively. Against God it is blasphemy (9:3; 26:65); here it is used of insults hurled at Jesus.

decisions.choice: shaking their heads: Psalm 22:7 (22:8 in the Hebrew numbering)
decisions.reason: The psalm says: all who see me mock me; they shake their heads. It was a gesture of scorn (Lamentations 2:15).

decisions.choice: you who destroy the temple and build it: the charge of 26:61
decisions.reason: The passersby repeat the words reported at the night hearing (26:61). In John 2:19-21 Jesus spoke of the temple of his body.

decisions.choice: If you are the Son of God: the tempter's words in 4:3 and 4:6
decisions.reason: The mockers use the very words the devil used when he urged Jesus to prove himself.

decisions.choice: the title turned into an exclamation (B) or a statement (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn the mocking title into words that sound natural in a taunt.

records.source: ὁμοίως καὶ οἱ ἀρχιερεῖς ἐμπαίζοντες μετὰ τῶν γραμματέων καὶ πρεσβυτέρων ἔλεγον·
records.gloss: Likewise also the chief priests mocking with the scribes and elders were saying,
pieces: In the same way the chief priests made fun of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, along with the scribes and the elders. They said,

L.41: In the same way the chief priests also, mocking [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] together with the scribes and elders, were saying,

R.41: The leading priests, the teachers of the law, and the elders also made fun of Jesus. They said,

decisions.choice: the chief priests, scribes and elders: the groups that made up the council
decisions.reason: These are the three groups Jesus named when he foretold his suffering (16:21). The leaders themselves come to mock.

decisions.choice: were saying: they kept saying
decisions.reason: The tense shows mockery that went on.

records.source: Ἄλλους ἔσωσεν, ἑαυτὸν οὐ δύναται σῶσαι· βασιλεὺς Ἰσραήλ ἐστιν, καταβάτω νῦν ἀπὸ τοῦ σταυροῦ καὶ πιστεύσομεν ἐπ’ αὐτόν.
records.gloss: Others he saved, himself not he is able to save; King of Israel he is, let him come down now from the cross and we will believe in him.
pieces: "He saved others, yet {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} has no power to save {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}. The King of Israel, is {{deity_pronoun:he|He}}? Then let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} come down off the cross this moment, and we will believe in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.42: "Others {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} saved; {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}} {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is not able to save. He is [the] King of Israel; let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} come down now from the cross, and we will believe in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.42: "He saved other people, but {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} cannot save {{deity_pronoun:himself|Himself}}! So {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is the King of Israel! Then let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} come down from the cross now. If {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} does, we will believe in {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: he saved others; himself he cannot save: true in a way the mockers do not see
decisions.reason: The leaders mean it as scorn. Yet Jesus came to save his people from their sins (1:21), and he gives his life for many (20:28). To save others he does not save himself (compare 16:25).

decisions.choice: He is King of Israel: spoken in scorn
decisions.reason: The leaders say "King of Israel", the name Israel's own people would use, not the Roman "King of the Jews". They say it to mock.

decisions.choice: believe in him: trust him as the one he claims to be
decisions.reason: They promise faith if he gives them the proof they demand, as the leaders asked for a sign before (12:38; 16:1).

decisions.choice: a mocking question (B) or exclamation (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable bring out the scorn in the statement.

records.source: πέποιθεν ἐπὶ τὸν θεόν, ῥυσάσθω νῦν εἰ θέλει αὐτόν· εἶπεν γὰρ ὅτι Θεοῦ εἰμι υἱός.
records.gloss: He has trusted on the God, let him rescue now if he wants him; he said for that, Of God I am Son.
pieces: He put {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} trust in God, so let God rescue {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} now, if God really wants {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. For {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, 'I am God's Son.'"

L.43: He has trusted in God; let {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} rescue [{{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}] now if {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} wants {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}; for {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, 'I am God's Son.'"

R.43: He trusts God. So let God save {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} now, if God really wants {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. After all, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} said, 'I am God's Son.'"

decisions.choice: he trusted in God; let him rescue him: Psalm 22:8 (22:9 in the Hebrew numbering)
decisions.reason: The psalm puts these words in the mouths of the sufferer's enemies: he trusted in the Lord, let him rescue him, since he delights in him. The leaders unknowingly take the enemies' part in the psalm. In the psalm the Hebrew has God's name.

decisions.choice: if he wants him: if God takes pleasure in him
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to want or to delight in, as in the Greek of Psalm 22:8. God had already said he delights in his Son (3:17).

decisions.choice: I am God's Son: the claim that Jesus is the Son of God
alternatives: I am a son of God
decisions.reason: The words recall the charge at the night hearing (26:63-64). The mockers turn Jesus's claim against him.

decisions.choice: God
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name God, so that the reader can tell who is meant. Pronouns for God and for Jesus take the deity_pronoun setting at every level, even in the mouths of his enemies.

records.source: τὸ δ’ αὐτὸ καὶ οἱ λῃσταὶ οἱ συσταυρωθέντες σὺν αὐτῷ ὠνείδιζον αὐτόν.
records.gloss: The and same also the bandits the [ones] crucified with him were reviling him.
pieces: Even the bandits crucified alongside {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} heaped the same insults on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.44: And in the same way the bandits who were crucified with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} also reproached {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

R.44: Even the robbers who were on the crosses next to Jesus insulted {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} in the same way.

decisions.choice: the bandits: both of them
decisions.reason: Matthew speaks of the two men together. Luke 23:39-43 tells that one of them later rebuked the other; Matthew does not tell that part.

decisions.choice: reproached: heaped abuse on
decisions.reason: The verb means to insult or put to shame (5:11).

records.source: Ἀπὸ δὲ ἕκτης ὥρας σκότος ἐγένετο ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν ἕως ὥρας ἐνάτης.
records.gloss: From then sixth hour darkness came over all the land until hour ninth.
pieces: At noon darkness fell over the whole land, and it lasted until three in the afternoon.

L.45: Now from [the] sixth hour darkness came over all the land until [the] ninth hour.

R.45: At twelve o'clock noon, the whole land became dark. It stayed dark until three o'clock in the afternoon.

decisions.choice: the sixth hour, the ninth hour: about noon and about three in the afternoon
decisions.reason: Jews and Romans counted the hours of daylight from sunrise, about six in the morning (20:3-6).

decisions.choice: the land: the land of Israel, or the whole earth
decisions.reason: The same word can mean land or earth. Matthew does not say how far the darkness reached.

decisions.choice: darkness: a sign of God's judgment
decisions.reason: Amos 8:9 says that on that day God will make the sun go down at noon. Darkness also covered Egypt before the Passover (Exodus 10:22). Passover fell at full moon, when an eclipse of the sun cannot happen.

decisions.choice: noon, three in the afternoon (B); twelve o'clock noon, three o'clock in the afternoon (R)
alternatives: the sixth hour, the ninth hour
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the ancient way of counting the hours. Balanced and Readable give the time as we count it, as in Mark 15:33.

records.heading: The death of Jesus

records.source: περὶ δὲ τὴν ἐνάτην ὥραν ἀνεβόησεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς φωνῇ μεγάλῃ λέγων· Ἠλὶ ἠλὶ λεμὰ σαβαχθάνι;
records.gloss: About then the ninth hour cried out the Jesus with voice loud saying, Eli eli lema sabachthani?
pieces: At about three o'clock Jesus gave a loud cry: "Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?"

L.46: And about the ninth hour Jesus cried out with a loud voice, saying, "Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?"

R.46: At about three o'clock Jesus shouted loudly, "Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani?"

decisions.choice: Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani: the first line of Psalm 22, Psalm 22:1 (22:2 in the Hebrew numbering)
decisions.reason: Jesus prays the opening of Psalm 22. The psalm moves from a cry of being forsaken to praise of God who rescues, at its end. Matthew has already echoed it in 27:35, 39 and 43.

decisions.choice: Eli ... sabachthani: the Hebrew form for my God, with an Aramaic verb
decisions.reason: Eli is close to the Hebrew of the psalm; sabachthani is Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Jesus's land. Mark 15:34 has the Aramaic Eloi. The sound of Eli explains why some heard the name Elijah (27:47).

decisions.choice: the spelling of the SBLGNT
decisions.reason: Manuscripts spell these words in several ways, some matching Mark. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani
decisions.reason: All levels keep the words in Latin letters, following the SBLGNT spelling, as Matthew keeps them and then translates them. The misunderstanding in 27:47 depends on their sound. Balanced and Readable give the hour as three o'clock, as in 27:45.

records.source: τοῦτ’ ἔστιν· Θεέ μου θεέ μου, ἱνατί με ἐγκατέλιπες;
records.gloss: That is, God of me, God of me, why me you forsook?
pieces: That means, "My God, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} God, why have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} abandoned {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

L.46: That is, "My God, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} God, why have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} forsaken {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?"

R.46: These words mean, "My God, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} God, why have {{deity_pronoun:you|You}} left {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} all alone?"

decisions.choice: my God: Jesus speaks to God
decisions.reason: Jesus addresses God and calls him "my God". Even in the cry of being forsaken he holds on to God as his own.

decisions.choice: forsaken: left behind, abandoned
decisions.reason: The verb means to leave someone alone in a time of need.

decisions.choice: the cry: Jesus's real anguish
decisions.reason: The words are a real cry of suffering, spoken in the words of Scripture. Matthew does not explain it further.

decisions.choice: my, you, me take the deity_pronoun setting
decisions.reason: "My" and "me" are Jesus speaking of himself, and "you" is God. The first "My" starts the quoted sentence and is written plain. Readable uses plain words for forsaken.

records.source: τινὲς δὲ τῶν ἐκεῖ ἑστηκότων ἀκούσαντες ἔλεγον ὅτι Ἠλίαν φωνεῖ οὗτος.
records.gloss: Some then of those there standing having heard were saying that Elijah calls this one.
pieces: Hearing it, some of those who stood nearby said, "This fellow is calling for Elijah!"

L.47: And some of those standing there, when they heard [it], were saying, "This [man] is calling Elijah."

R.47: Some of the people standing there heard {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. They said, "He is calling for Elijah!"

decisions.choice: Elijah: the prophet God promised to send
decisions.reason: God promised to send Elijah before the great day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5; 3:23 in the Hebrew). Jesus spoke of this in 11:14 and 17:10-13.

decisions.choice: calling Elijah: misheard, or twisted in mockery
decisions.reason: Eli sounds like the name Elijah. Whether they misheard or twisted his words to mock him, Matthew does not say.

decisions.choice: this one: perhaps said with scorn
decisions.reason: The pronoun can carry contempt, as "this fellow" does.

decisions.choice: this fellow
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out the tone of the pronoun.

records.source: καὶ εὐθέως δραμὼν εἷς ἐξ αὐτῶν καὶ λαβὼν σπόγγον πλήσας τε ὄξους καὶ περιθεὶς καλάμῳ ἐπότιζεν αὐτόν.
records.gloss: And immediately having run one of them and having taken a sponge having filled and with sour wine and having put on a reed was giving to drink him.
pieces: At once one of them ran and got a sponge. He soaked it in sour wine, put it on the end of a stick, and held it up for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} to drink.

L.48: And immediately one of them ran and took a sponge, filled [it] with sour wine, put [it] on a reed, and was giving {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} a drink.

R.48: Right away one of them ran and got a sponge. He filled it with cheap sour wine and put it on the end of a stick. Then he held it up to Jesus's mouth so {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} could drink.

decisions.choice: sour wine: cheap wine gone sour, a common drink
decisions.reason: Soldiers and laborers drank this sharp wine mixed with water. It eased thirst.

decisions.choice: sour wine to drink: Psalm 69:21 (69:22 in the Hebrew numbering)
decisions.reason: The psalm says: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.

decisions.choice: the drink: whether kind or cruel is not clear
decisions.reason: The man may have meant to help, or to keep Jesus alive a little longer to see if Elijah came (27:49). Matthew does not say.

decisions.choice: stick
decisions.reason: As in 27:29, Balanced and Readable say stick. Readable adds "cheap" to say what kind of wine it was.

records.source: οἱ δὲ λοιποὶ ἔλεγον· Ἄφες ἴδωμεν εἰ ἔρχεται Ἠλίας σώσων αὐτόν.
records.gloss: The but rest were saying, Leave, let us see whether comes Elijah saving him.
pieces: But the rest told him, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to save {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

L.49: But the rest were saying, "Leave [it]; let us see whether Elijah comes to save {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

R.49: But the others said, "Stop! Let us wait and see if Elijah will come and save {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}."

decisions.choice: Leave: wait, hold off
decisions.reason: The word means let go or allow. Here it most likely means hold off and wait. It may also simply introduce "let us see".

decisions.choice: the SBLGNT ends the verse here
alternatives: some important early manuscripts add: and another took a spear and pierced his side, and water and blood came out
decisions.reason: Some early manuscripts, including two of the oldest complete copies of the Greek Bible, add these words, which are like John 19:34. They would place the piercing before Jesus died. Most manuscripts do not have them, and the SBLGNT leaves them out. Reviewers should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: to save him: the purpose of Elijah's coming
decisions.reason: The form shows purpose: whether Elijah comes in order to save him.

records.source: ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς πάλιν κράξας φωνῇ μεγάλῃ ἀφῆκεν τὸ πνεῦμα.
records.gloss: The but Jesus again having cried out with voice loud let go the spirit.
pieces: Once more Jesus cried out with a loud voice, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} yielded up {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} spirit.

L.50: And Jesus cried out again with a loud voice and yielded up [{{deity_pronoun:his|His}}] spirit.

R.50: Jesus shouted loudly again. Then {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gave up {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} spirit and died.

decisions.choice: yielded up his spirit: let his spirit go, and so died
alternatives: his spirit was taken from him
decisions.reason: The verb means to let go or send away. The wording suggests that Jesus gave up his life himself rather than having it taken (compare 20:28; John 10:18). It may also be simply a way of saying he died.

decisions.choice: again: a second loud cry, after 27:46
decisions.reason: Matthew does not give the words of this cry.

decisions.choice: spirit: his life, his human spirit
decisions.reason: The word means breath, life or spirit. Here it is Jesus's own life given up in death.

decisions.choice: and died
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that Jesus died.

records.source: καὶ ἰδοὺ τὸ καταπέτασμα τοῦ ναοῦ ἐσχίσθη ἀπ’ ἄνωθεν ἕως κάτω εἰς δύο, καὶ ἡ γῆ ἐσείσθη, καὶ αἱ πέτραι ἐσχίσθησαν, καὶ τὰ μνημεῖα ἀνεῴχθησαν καὶ πολλὰ σώματα τῶν κεκοιμημένων ἁγίων ἠγέρθησαν, καὶ ἐξελθόντες ἐκ τῶν μνημείων μετὰ τὴν ἔγερσιν αὐτοῦ εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν πόλιν καὶ ἐνεφανίσθησαν πολλοῖς.
records.gloss: And behold, the curtain of the temple was torn from above to below into two, and the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split, \v 52 and the tombs were opened and many bodies of the having fallen asleep holy ones were raised, \v 53 and having come out of the tombs after the raising of him they entered into the holy city and appeared to many.
pieces: Then the temple curtain split in two, from the top all the way to the bottom. The ground shook and rocks were torn apart.
Graves were opened, and the bodies of many of God's holy people who had fallen asleep in death were raised.
Coming out of the graves after Jesus was raised, they went into the holy city and showed themselves to many people.

L.51: And look, the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom, and the earth was shaken, and the rocks were split,
L.52: and the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the holy ones who had fallen asleep were raised,
L.53: and coming out of the tombs after {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} raising, they went into the holy city and appeared to many.

R.51: At that moment the curtain in the temple was torn into two pieces, from the top to the bottom. The ground shook, and rocks split apart.
R.52: Graves broke open, and many of God's people who had died were brought back to life.
R.53: They came out of their graves. After Jesus came back to life, they went into Jerusalem, the holy city, and many people saw them.

decisions.choice: the curtain of the temple: most likely the inner curtain before the Most Holy Place
alternatives: the outer curtain at the entrance
decisions.reason: The sanctuary had two great curtains. The inner one closed off the Most Holy Place, where only the high priest went once a year (Exodus 26:31-33; Hebrews 10:19-20). The outer one hung at the entrance. Matthew does not say which, or explain the sign; the passive and "from top to bottom" point to God as the one who tore it.

decisions.choice: after his raising: with coming out, or with entering the city
alternatives: the holy ones came out after Jesus rose
they came out at his death and entered the city after he rose
decisions.reason: The phrase stands between "coming out of the tombs" and "went into the holy city" and may belong with either. Either way, Jesus is the first to rise (1 Corinthians 15:20).

decisions.choice: the holy ones who had fallen asleep: faithful people of God who had died
decisions.reason: Sleep is a picture of death for those who will rise (Daniel 12:2; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-14). Ezekiel 37:12-13 pictures God opening his people's graves. Matthew does not say who these were or what became of them.

decisions.choice: the holy city: Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Matthew called Jerusalem the holy city in 4:5.

decisions.choice: look (L); at that moment (R); then (B) (B, R)
decisions.reason: As in 1:20, Literal uses "look" and Balanced and Readable carry the word's force in the flow of the sentence.

decisions.choice: after Jesus was raised (B); after Jesus came back to life (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name Jesus and use a verb instead of the noun. Readable names Jerusalem.

records.source: Ὁ δὲ ἑκατόνταρχος καὶ οἱ μετ’ αὐτοῦ τηροῦντες τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἰδόντες τὸν σεισμὸν καὶ τὰ γενόμενα ἐφοβήθησαν σφόδρα λέγοντες· Ἀληθῶς θεοῦ υἱὸς ἦν οὗτος.
records.gloss: The but centurion and those with him keeping watch over the Jesus having seen the earthquake and the things happening feared greatly saying, Truly God's Son was this.
pieces: The centurion and the men with him who were guarding Jesus saw the earthquake and everything that was happening, and they were filled with fear. "This man truly was God's Son!" they said.

L.54: And when the centurion and those with him who were keeping watch over Jesus saw the earthquake and the things that were happening, they were greatly afraid, saying, "Truly this was God's Son!"

R.54: The Roman army officer and the soldiers with him were guarding Jesus. They saw the earthquake and everything else that happened, and they were very afraid. They said, "This man really was God's Son!"

decisions.choice: God's Son: the Son of God
decisions.reason: The Greek has no article, so it could mean "a son of God" or, from Gentiles, "a son of a god". But a title placed before the verb often lacks the article and is still definite, and the words answer the mockers' "if you are the Son of God" (27:40, 43). The disciples said the same words in 14:33. What the soldiers themselves understood is less certain.

decisions.choice: centurion: a Roman officer over about a hundred soldiers
decisions.reason: He was in charge of the execution, like the centurion of 8:5 a Gentile.

decisions.choice: greatly afraid: struck with awe
decisions.reason: The fear comes from seeing God at work, as with the disciples in 17:6.

decisions.choice: God's Son
decisions.reason: All levels say "God's Son", which keeps the openness of the Greek. Readable says "Roman army officer" for centurion, as in 8:5.

records.source: Ἦσαν δὲ ἐκεῖ γυναῖκες πολλαὶ ἀπὸ μακρόθεν θεωροῦσαι, αἵτινες ἠκολούθησαν τῷ Ἰησοῦ ἀπὸ τῆς Γαλιλαίας διακονοῦσαι αὐτῷ·
records.gloss: Were then there women many from afar watching, who followed the Jesus from the Galilee serving him;
pieces: A number of women stood watching from far off. These women had come with Jesus all the way from Galilee, providing for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

L.55: And many women were there, watching from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, serving {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}};

R.55: Many women were there too. They watched from far away. They had followed Jesus from Galilee to help {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and take care of {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}.

decisions.choice: serving him: providing for his needs
decisions.reason: The verb means to serve or wait on. Luke 8:3 says such women provided for Jesus from their own means.

decisions.choice: the women stayed when the disciples fled
decisions.reason: All the disciples had left him and fled (26:56). The women watch his death, his burial (27:61) and the empty tomb (28:1).

decisions.choice: from a distance: perhaps Psalm 38:11 (38:12 in the Hebrew numbering)
decisions.reason: The psalm says that friends and neighbors stand far off. Matthew does not cite it.

records.source: ἐν αἷς ἦν Μαρία ἡ Μαγδαληνὴ καὶ Μαρία ἡ τοῦ Ἰακώβου καὶ Ἰωσὴφ μήτηρ καὶ ἡ μήτηρ τῶν υἱῶν Ζεβεδαίου.
records.gloss: among whom was Mary the Magdalene and Mary the of James and Joseph mother and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.
pieces: Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of Zebedee's sons.

L.56: among whom were Mary the Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.

R.56: Mary from the town of Magdala was there. So was Mary, the mother of James and Joseph. The mother of James and John, the sons of Zebedee, was there too.

decisions.choice: Mary the Magdalene: Mary from Magdala
decisions.reason: Magdala was a town on the west shore of the Sea of Galilee. Luke 8:2 says seven demons had gone out of her.

decisions.choice: Mary the mother of James and Joseph: most likely not Jesus's mother
decisions.reason: Jesus had brothers named James and Joseph (13:55), but Matthew would hardly name Jesus's mother this way here. Mark 15:40 calls this Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses.

decisions.choice: the mother of Zebedee's sons: the mother of James and John
decisions.reason: She asked Jesus for places at his right and left (20:20-21). Mark 15:40 names a Salome among the women; she may be the same person.

decisions.choice: from the town of Magdala; James and John
alternatives: the Magdalene; the sons of Zebedee
decisions.reason: Readable explains the name and names the sons of Zebedee (4:21).

records.source: Ὀψίας δὲ γενομένης ἦλθεν ἄνθρωπος πλούσιος ἀπὸ Ἁριμαθαίας, τοὔνομα Ἰωσήφ, ὃς καὶ αὐτὸς ἐμαθητεύθη τῷ Ἰησοῦ·
records.gloss: Evening then having come came a man rich from Arimathea, the name Joseph, who also himself was discipled to the Jesus;
pieces: As evening came on, Joseph arrived, a rich man from the town of Arimathea who had also become one of Jesus's disciples.

L.57: And when evening had come, a rich man from Arimathea came, named Joseph, who himself also had become a disciple of Jesus;

R.57: That evening a rich man named Joseph came. He was from the town of Arimathea. He had also become a follower of Jesus.

decisions.choice: evening: the late afternoon before sunset, with the Sabbath near
decisions.reason: The law said a body hanged on a tree must not stay there overnight (Deuteronomy 21:22-23), and the Sabbath began at sunset (27:62).

decisions.choice: Arimathea: a town in Judea
decisions.reason: Luke 23:51 calls it a town of the Jews. Its exact location is not certain.

decisions.choice: a rich man: perhaps Isaiah 53:9
decisions.reason: The servant in Isaiah 53:9 is with a rich man in his death. Matthew does not cite the verse.

decisions.choice: had become a disciple: had been taught by Jesus and followed him
decisions.reason: The verb means to be made a disciple (28:19). John 19:38 says Joseph followed Jesus in secret.

decisions.choice: follower
decisions.reason: Readable uses an everyday word for disciple, as elsewhere in Matthew.
